name: Call log, SMS and messages
plain: Web pages cannot read calls, texts or messages on the device.
meaning: No browser API exposes call history or SMS inboxes. WebOTP reads a single matching code. Android native apps need READ_SMS and READ_CALL_LOG; Google Play restricts both heavily.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: proxy: WebOTP
fields.range: single code from a matching SMS, only if SMS names the site origin

limits.headline: Can't see your calls, texts, or messages from a web page
limits.user_action: Nothing. Pages have no way to ask for this
can: Take one matching one time code from a text on Android (WebOTP)
Fill a code you type in yourself
Ask you to paste a code
cannot: Get around store rules; Google Play restricts SMS and call log access for apps
limits.differs: Android apps can ask for SMS and call log access, but Google Play limits it. Web pages cannot.

story.what_it_is: Web pages cannot read your calls, texts or messages.

marketing.name: WebOTP API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes a way to receive one verification code by SMS after you approve it.

story.for_you: A website cannot see who you called or what people texted you. If you sign in with a texted code, the browser may offer to fill that one code after you approve it.
story.for_makers: Apps wanted message access to read codes, spot scams and learn about contacts. On the web there is no such access, only one narrow route for verification codes. Native apps need special permissions that app stores restrict.

use_cases.example: A bank login wanted to read the texted code on its own. It now relies on the single code filled in after you tap.
A payment page wanted to confirm a code by scanning messages and uses the one time code route.
A chat site wanted to find friends from your call log and asks you to share contacts through a picker.
A delivery site wanted to read your texts for tracking links and uses its own notifications.
A scammer page wanted to see your messages, which is why web pages have no such route.
A web messaging app wanted to show your texts and only works with its own chats.
An advertiser wanted your call frequency as a signal of lifestyle, which is not available.

risks: Only a single code can be read
Native apps get far more access

legit_uses: None: the browser deliberately withholds it
abuse: Sites attempt proxies to recover it
